897.title: Mourning as devotion
897.hook: in Muharram many Shia communities hold majalis, recite elegies and serve water
897.howItsDone: In Muharram, Shia communities hold majalis, gatherings where a speaker retells Karbala and reciters chant elegies, and some set out water and food for passersby in Husayn's memory.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ghaybah, the awaited Imam: the Twelver Shia belief that the twelfth Imam is hidden and will return. Your line was: awaiting justice. Where did you wait for something to be put right? Day eight hundred ninety-seven.

A hall with the lights turned low. Black cloth on the walls. People sit on the floor, shoulder to shoulder, and someone at the front begins to speak, slowly, about a camp by a river. Halfway through, a voice rises into a chant, and the room answers it. Some people beat their chests in rhythm. Some cover their faces. Outside the door, a table with jugs of water and cups for anyone walking past. This is a majlis in Muharram, and in Shia communities it can happen night after night. To an outsider it can look like grief that will not end. Shia teachers call it something closer to love. Today: mourning as devotion.

Start with the word. A majlis is simply a sitting, a gathering. In Muharram it becomes a gathering to remember Husayn. A speaker retells Karbala, often one person or one moment each night: the thirst, al-Abbas at the river, Zaynab's voice. Then come the elegies, poems of grief sung or chanted, and the room weeps. Why weep for someone who died so long ago? Shia teachers answer: because we love him, and because the Prophet ﷺ loved him. Tears for Husayn are tears for the Prophet's own grandson, and so they are a way of standing with the Prophet's family. The weeping is the point, not a side effect. And tears themselves have a place in Islam. When the Prophet's infant son Ibrahim was dying, the hadith says, the Prophet's eyes filled with tears. Someone was surprised. He said, in effect: the eye weeps and the heart grieves, but we say only what pleases our Lord. Grief is not a failure of faith. The Qur'an gives the words believers say when loss arrives: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." Mourning, held like this, faces God rather than turning away. Then the water. Because the camp at Karbala was kept from the river, Shia communities in Muharram set out water for strangers. A cup handed to someone you'll never see again becomes a small act of remembrance. Grief that ends in service. Grief as love.

The practice: serve water to someone. For now, settle and breathe. Bring to mind someone you have lost, or someone you love who is far away. Let the grief be there, without hurrying it off. Notice whose face comes with it. Breathe in. Breathe out. If you pray, you can ask God's mercy for that person, in your own words. Then, when the bell ends, pour a glass of water and hand it to someone: a family member, a coworker, a stranger. Say nothing about why. The bell holds the time.
Majlis, a sitting, a gathering: in Muharram, the gathering where Shia Muslims retell Karbala, weep for Husayn, and set out water, offering grief itself as love. Today's word.
Your line: grief as love. Today, when a sad memory comes, let it point you to the person you loved. Then do one small kindness in their name. Day eight hundred ninety-seven.

898.title: The four in Sunni reckoning
898.hook: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, Ali: the Rightly Guided Caliphs for Sunni Muslims
898.howItsDone: Sunni Muslims name Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali together as the Rightly Guided Caliphs, often adding 'may God be pleased with him' after each name, and some Friday sermons mention all four.

segments.voice: Yesterday, majlis, mourning as devotion: the majalis of Muharram, the elegies, the water at the door. Your line was: grief as love. Whose memory did you carry into a small kindness? Day eight hundred ninety-eight.

Four names, in order. Abu Bakr. Umar. Uthman. Ali. Over the last few weeks, each one has had his own days here: a first speech, a register, a single reading of the Qur'an, a shield brought before a judge. Now the path steps back and starts gathering the story up. Because in Sunni Islam, those four names are also said together, in that order, as one group with one title. In a Friday sermon, the preacher may name all four and ask God to be pleased with them. Today: the four in Sunni reckoning.

The title is al-khulafa' al-rashidun: the rightly guided caliphs. Khulafa' is the plural of khalifah, successor, the one who comes after. Rashidun means rightly guided, people who walk on the straight road. The phrase leans on a hadith. In it, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ gives his companions a farewell counsel: hold to my way, and the way of the rightly guided successors after me, and grip it tightly. Sunni scholars read those successors as these four. This path has already traced how each of the four came to office, each by a different route. The Sunni telling looks at those four doors and sees one community walking through all of them, so the four belong together, in that order. Their time is held up as the model of what rule under God should look like, even with its wars and its grief. Here is the detail worth keeping. Ali stands fourth in this Sunni list. And in Shia Islam, Ali stands first, as the first Imam. The same man, honored in both, counted from a different place. Sunni Muslims love Ali as the fourth of the four and as the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law. Shia Muslims love him as the one the Prophet named. Neither side leaves him out. Tomorrow turns to the family everyone loves. Today, the four.

The practice: say their names. Settle, and let your breathing slow. Then say the four names, quietly, in order, one per breath. Abu Bakr. Umar. Uthman. Ali. With each name, bring back one thing you remember from his days on this path: a speech, a register, a page, a shield. In Sunni practice, each name is followed by: may God be pleased with him. If you pray, you can add it too. Then go round the four again, slower. The bell holds the time.
Al-khulafa' al-rashidun. The rightly guided caliphs: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali, named together, in order, in Sunni Islam. Today's word.
Your line: the four. Today, think of four people who came before you in your family or your work, in order. Say their names once, with thanks. Day eight hundred ninety-eight.

899.title: The family, loved by all
899.hook: every prayer asks blessings on Muhammad and the family of Muhammad
899.howItsDone: In the sitting of the daily prayer, Sunni and Shia Muslims ask blessings on Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, and the short salawat is also said when the Prophet's name is mentioned.

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-khulafa' al-rashidun: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali, the rightly guided caliphs in Sunni reckoning. Your line was: the four. Whose four names did you say with thanks? Day eight hundred ninety-nine.

The companions had a question. They already knew how to greet the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: peace be upon you. But the Qur'an had told them something more, to ask blessings on him. So how, exactly? What words? The hadith says he answered them with a short prayer, and it did not stop at his own name. It reached past him, to his family. Those words travel into the prayer itself. Today: the family, loved by all.
screen: `HOW DO WE ASK BLESSINGS ON YOU?`

segments.voice: Begin with the verse behind the question. The Qur'an says: "Lo! Allah and His angels shower blessings on the Prophet. O ye who believe! Ask blessings on him and salute him with a worthy salutation." When the companions asked how, the hadith in al-Bukhari gives his reply. In its opening words: O God, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed Abraham and the family of Abraham. Notice two things. First, the family is in the prayer by the Prophet's own choice. He was asked about himself and he added them. Second, he set it beside Abraham and his household, a family the Qur'an itself honors. The Arabic phrase is al Muhammad, the family of Muhammad. Scholars discuss who it includes. In Shia teaching it points above all to Ali, Fatimah, Hasan and Husayn, and the Imams after them. Sunni scholars have read it as his household, some more widely. But the love is shared. Words from this prayer are said in the sitting of the daily prayer, in Sunni and Shia practice alike. A poem attributed to the Sunni jurist al-Shafi'i says, in effect: O family of God's Messenger, love of you is a duty God revealed. After weeks of a hard story, here is a place where Sunni and Shia Muslims say the same names in the same breath. On him and his family.
screen: then, large: `ON HIM AND HIS FAMILY.`

segments.voice: The practice: say the salawat, meaning it. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, you can say the short blessing known as the salawat: Allahumma salli ala Muhammad wa ala ali Muhammad. O God, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad. Say it slowly, once per breath. On the word family, bring to mind the names: Ali, Fatimah, Hasan, Husayn. If you don't pray, simply hold those names in mind, one per breath, and let them be people rather than titles. The bell holds the time.
The family. Al Muhammad, the household of the Prophet, whom he named in the blessing he taught, and whom Sunni and Shia Muslims both love. Today's word.
Your line: on him and his family. Today, when you thank someone, thank their people too: the parent, the partner, the team behind them. Day eight hundred ninety-nine.

900.title: What is shared
900.hook: one Allah, one Prophet ﷺ, one Qur'an, one qiblah, five prayers
900.howItsDone: Sunni and Shia Muslims share the Qur'an, the five daily prayers facing the Kaaba, the Ramadan fast and the pilgrimage to Mecca; differences such as hand position or combining prayer times sit within that shared practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the family: the blessing the Prophet taught, reaching past him to his household, said in prayer by Sunni and Shia alike. Your line was: on him and his family. Whose people did you thank? Day nine hundred.

Try a short list. One God. One Prophet, Muhammad ﷺ. One Qur'an, the same words in the same order. One direction to face, the Kaaba in Mecca. Prayer, day and night, bowing and putting the forehead to the ground. The fast of Ramadan. The pilgrimage to the same house, walking around it in the same direction. That list is true for a Sunni Muslim in one city and a Shia Muslim in another. For weeks this path has followed a split. Today the path counts the other column. Today: what is shared.

Here is a hadith in al-Bukhari that draws the line with almost nothing. The Prophet said, in effect: whoever prays our prayer, faces our qiblah, and eats what we slaughter, that one is a Muslim, under the protection of God and His Messenger. Three plain, outward things: a prayer, a direction, a meal. That is the whole measure this report gives. Then the Qur'an: "And hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate." A rope, held by many hands. The verse does not ask everyone to stand in the same spot on the rope. It asks them to keep holding it. Now the qiblah. The word means the direction you face. Muslims in prayer turn toward the same house, so the rows of the whole world, if you could see them from above, would form rings around one center. Sunni and Shia alike. Even the differences sit inside the shared. Sunni and Shia Muslims both pray the five daily prayers; Shia practice allows gathering them into three times of day, and Sunni schools allow joining them in certain cases, such as travel. Tomorrow looks at the smaller differences you can see in a row of worshipers; they too sit inside one prayer, facing one way. The split was real, and the grief was real. But set the two lists side by side, and see which one runs longer. More shared than split.

The practice: list what you share with every Muslim. If you are Muslim, count it out on your fingers, slowly, one item per breath: God, the Prophet, the Qur'an, the qiblah, the prayer, the fast, the pilgrimage. If you're not, make the same kind of list with someone you differ from: a neighbor, a relative, a coworker. What do you both love, both fear, both hope for? Let the list grow longer than you expected. The bell holds the time.
Qiblah, the direction faced in prayer: toward the Kaaba, the same for Sunni and Shia Muslims, alongside one God, one Prophet, one Qur'an, and one prayer. Today's word.
Your line: more shared than split. Today, when someone irritates you, name one thing you have in common before you answer. Day nine hundred.

901.title: Sunni and Shia today
901.hook: Sunni and Shia Muslims today, two families of one faith, praying side by side
901.tomorrow: Block C close: the wound and the healing
901.howItsDone: Sunni and Shia Muslims perform the same pilgrimage rites in Mecca, and in some cities pray in the same mosques; Shia worshipers prostrate on earth, such as a clay tablet, and pray with arms at their sides, as some Maliki Sunnis also do.

segments.voice: Yesterday, qiblah: one God, one Prophet, one Qur'an, one qiblah, one prayer. Your line was: more shared than split. What did you find you had in common with someone? Day nine hundred one.

A row of people in prayer, shoulder to shoulder. The man on the left has his hands folded over his chest. The man on the right lets his arms hang at his sides. When they go down into prostration, one of them sets his forehead on a small disc of baked clay he carried in his pocket. The other puts his forehead straight on the carpet. Then they rise, at the same moment, facing the same way. From the back of the room you might guess one is Sunni and one is Shia. You might be wrong. Today: Sunni and Shia today.

Sunni and Shia Muslims share cities, streets, and sometimes houses. Here's what side by side looks like. At the pilgrimage in Mecca, pilgrims from both walk around the same Kaaba, stand on the same plain of Arafat, and throw stones at the same pillars. No one checks which telling of the succession you hold. In some cities there are mosques where both pray in the same rows. In some families, a Sunni mother and a Shia father, or the reverse, raise children who know both ways of standing. The differences you can see are small and real. Shia practice is to pray with arms at the sides and to prostrate on natural earth, such as a clay tablet called a turbah, since Shia jurists teach that the forehead should rest on earth or what grows from it. Folded hands are the Sunni posture people tend to picture. But in the Maliki school of Sunni law, praying with arms at the sides is an accepted practice too. So the hands alone sort nobody. And scholars of the schools, Sunni and Shia, have put their names to a statement issued in Amman, recognizing one another's schools as Muslim and saying that their followers may not be declared outside the faith. Statements don't end every quarrel. But they say where the scholars chose to stand. Side by side.

The practice: pray beside someone different. If you pray, the next time you are in a mosque, stand in the row next to whoever is there, without guessing who they are. For now, sit and breathe. Picture a line of people in prayer, each one standing a little differently, all of them facing one way. Put yourself in the line. Then bring to mind someone you live or work beside who sees the world differently from you. Breathe in. Breathe out. Stand with them, in your mind, for a moment. The bell holds the time.

Turbah, earth or soil: the clay tablet some Shia worshipers rest their foreheads on in prostration, one of the small, visible differences between Sunni and Shia Muslims who pray in the same rows. Today's word.
Your line: side by side. Today, sit or stand next to someone you'd usually avoid, and leave the difference unspoken. Day nine hundred one.

902.title: Block C close: the wound and the healing
902.hook: a split remembered with grief, and a family everyone loves
902.howItsDone: Sunni and Shia Muslims remember the early conflicts in different ways, in sermons, histories and Muharram gatherings, and the Qur'an's prayer for 'our brethren who were before us in the faith' (59:10) is recited as a prayer against rancor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, turbah, Sunni and Shia today: hands folded and hands at the sides, one row, one Kaaba. Your line was: side by side. Who did you sit beside? Day nine hundred two.

This block began on the day after. The Prophet ﷺ had died, his body was not yet buried, and the community had to decide who would lead. Weeks later on this path, here we are. A pledge in a meeting hall. A pool called Ghadir Khumm. A calendar, a Coptic boy's case, a plague. A caliph killed at home, a battle around a camel, a field called Siffin. Hasan's peace, Husayn's refusal, a river cut off, Zaynab's voice. It is a hard stretch of history, and it has been told two ways. Today the block closes. Today: the wound and the healing.
screen: `A POOL, A CALENDAR, A FIELD, A RIVER.`

segments.voice: Start with the wound. The question of who should lead after the Prophet was answered one way by those who pledged to Abu Bakr and another way by those who held that the Prophet had named Ali. Out of those answers came the Sunni telling and the Shia telling, and both carried their grief: Uthman killed while reading the Qur'an, Ali struck in the mosque at Kufa, Husayn at Karbala. The wound is not hidden in either tradition. It is remembered, in sermons and in majalis. Now the healing, which was there all along. The same family is loved on both sides; the blessing on Muhammad and his family is said in prayer by both. The four caliphs and the twelve Imams have one man in common, Ali. The qiblah does not move for anyone. And the Qur'an gives words for people who come after an earlier generation. After praising the emigrants and the helpers of Medina, it describes believers who came later and say: "Our Lord! Forgive us and our brethren who were before us in the faith, and place not in our hearts any rancour toward those who believe." Notice what that prayer does. It does not settle who was right. It asks for forgiveness for everyone before us, and a heart without rancor toward everyone now. Read this way, unity is not an agreement reached. It is something asked for, again and again. Unity is a prayer. Next, the path leaves the split behind and walks into the cities the Muslims built.

The practice: pray for unity. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, you can say the Qur'an's words from today, slowly: Our Lord, forgive us and our brethren who were before us in the faith, and place not in our hearts any rancor toward those who believe. If you don't, bring to mind one rift you know, in a family, a friendship, a community, and simply hold both sides of it in mind without choosing. Breathe in for those who came before. Breathe out for those here now. The bell holds the time.
Ghill, rancor, a grudge in the heart: the word the Qur'an's prayer asks God to remove, closing this block on the wound of the first split and the healing held in common. Today's word.
Your line: unity is a prayer. Today, before you take a side in an old family argument, ask for good for both sides first. Day nine hundred two.

903.title: A capital in Damascus
903.hook: the Umayyads rule from Damascus over lands from Spain to Sindh
903.howItsDone: Muslim histories tell the Umayyad period, ruled from Damascus, as a time of wide expansion, and Sunni and Shia teachers judge its rulers differently.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ghill, Block C closed: the wound of the split and the healing held in common. Your line was: unity is a prayer. Which old quarrel did you wish good to both sides of? Day nine hundred three.

A new block, and a wider map. Put one finger on the Atlantic coast of Spain, where the land runs out into ocean. Put another on the Indus River, in Sindh, in what is now Pakistan. Between your fingers: North Africa, Egypt, Syria, Iraq, Persia. Under the Umayyad caliphs, one ruling house in Damascus claimed all of it. Arabs, Berbers, Copts, Greeks, Persians and many more, under one government. Block D begins: Islamic history and civilization. Today: a capital in Damascus.

The Umayyads are a clan of Quraysh, the Prophet's own tribe, and their line of caliphs began with Mu'awiyah. We met him already, ruling from Damascus. Today the path looks at what that seat became. Damascus was an old city long before Islam, a crossroads of caravans. From there, the Umayyad armies and governors pushed west across North Africa and into Spain, which Muslims called al-Andalus, and east into Central Asia and Sindh. That is the plain history: an empire, built partly by conquest, with all the costs conquest carries. The people of these lands did not all become Muslim at once. Churches and synagogues went on, and the histories suggest the change of faith came slowly, family by family. And a capital that rules so many peoples has a practical problem. How do you run it? At first, the answer was: keep the old offices. Clerks in Syria went on keeping records in Greek, as they had under Byzantium. Clerks in Iraq and Persia kept them in Persian. The Qur'an had already spoken to a world of many peoples: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." Nations and tribes, that they may know one another. A capital in Damascus held them under one roof, and from that mix came mosques, coins, books and cities. From Spain to Sindh.
